I don't understand the meaning behind your question. It's always been easy, so long as you could follow guides and recommendations.

Circa 2000-2013, so long as you had an nVidia card, was using their proprietary drivers, there weren't many problems. Is the game in the repo? Use yum or apt to install the game like any other package. Is it a third party game? Use their provided installer, usually in a .run file. After 2013, with Steam being released on Linux, use Steam like you do on Windows or MacOS. And now, if you are one of the retards that's still sucking ATI/AMD's dick, their open source drivers are getting close to performance parity with nVidia, though some games still don't work because of custom patches with nVidia to fix certain games (but, this is also true with Windows).

So, when you ask "Is it getting easier?" I don't know what you are talking about.

As for how is it these days? I now have more games than I can ever get to. My library is sitting at 558 games, with ~545 native to Linux (or supported by the developers to run on Linux). Steam has over 5000 games with the Linux icon, ProtonDB.com has 2700 Windows games reported as working out of the box with Proton, there is no shortage of good games that can be played on Linux.

I hear you but "easy" is a subjective term. I meant easy for like an end user who just wants to sit down and press install and play. I'm glad to hear that the actual available games has been expanding at what seems to be an increasing rate year over year. I was hoping personally that Steam OS would gain more traction because I felt that would convert a lot of people who are too scared to jump from Windows since like you said you can just install steam and install games like you normally would.

Linux games followed the same evolution as Windows game did. Before steam, you had installer files. Same as those .exe's you had, though for Linux it was either in a .run file (which was an installer that Ryan Gordon made when he worked for Loki) or they were a shell script (.sh). Running them, the game would get installed and you would usually get an icon on the desktop or menu to launch the game.

Sure, Steam made things easy to install games, but it still took some years before publishers stopped making physical copies. And even still, some still do make them today.

I would admit that the only times things got hard was when you wanted to install a game but there no installer, only the source code. Then you had to compile that shit by hand. That wasn't fun, but once you set up the builds, it's easy to automate that so you can easily compile newer versions. But then, you would find someone who has their own software repository that has the binaries for it. Hell, there were custom repo's for Ubuntu that had nothing but games on it, called play-deb. They did their best to provide games that weren't in the official Ubuntu repos. And then you have AUR for Arch users. But, I digress.

The point is, generally speaking, it's no harder than Windows was. And now, today, in some ways, it's actually easier (depending on the game and certain situations), Like not having to install directx on every games first launch and like how Valve get's more FPS's in Left 4 Dead 2 on Linux than on Windows, there are a lot of variables involved in finding out what works best.

I knew the Steam Machine was going to flop (not Steam OS, though, that's still being updated rather regularly). History has shone that when the software is released and third parties develop the hardware, the costs is too high and no one wants to buy it. We saw that with 3do. With one OS, but different hardware, no one knew what to buy and because it was so expensive, everyone stuch with their snes and genesis and waited for the n64 and playstation.

Everyone has their own theories as to why Valve is doing the whole Proton thing and IMO, it makes sense if they want to get into the Games as a Service business model. Needing a fuck ton of servers, it would be a billion times cheaper to run Linux servers and to use a translation layer to deliver the games than to pay Microsoft for a license for every instance. And if they can get 1 to 1 parity, even most Linux purists would have to say, "You know what, fuck it. I wanna play GTA6."
